newsitem.title: CHINA: FORECAST-Chinese yuan to move narrowly next month.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Chinese yuan to move narrowly next month.

text.p: The Chinese yuan will move narrowly against the U.S. dollar next month with an oversupply of dollars balanced by the pressure of possible central bank intervention to depresss the unit, analysts said on Sunday.
The yuan is likely to move between 8.2900 to 8.2930 against the U.S. dollar on the Shanghai-based China Foreign Exchange Trade System, a national foreign exchange market, analysts said.
On Friday, the yuan ended at 8.2908, just short of a two-year high close of 8.2892 reached on May 18, 1995.
"There is an oversupply of dollars in the market due to China's big trade surplus in the first half, continued foreign investment inflows and rising foreign exchange reserves," said a trader.
"But the yuan is now close to a two-year high level and the pressure of possible central bank intervention to depress it is mounting," he said.
China said last week that its foreign trade surplus surged to $17.77 billion in the first half of this year, against $876 million in the same period in 1996.

In the first half of this year, direct foreign investment hit $20.7 billion yuan, up a year-on-year 5.49 percent, the China Daily Business Weekly said on Sunday, quoting figures from the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation.
Analysts have said they believed actual foreign investment in China this year could maintain the $40 billion level reached last year.

China's foreign exchange reserves rose to $121.2 billion at the end of June against $105 billion at the start of this year, and officials have estimated reserves were likely to rise at least $20 billion this year.
"The yuan is under pressure to rise also because China's inflation has fallen sharply this year," a foreign exchange analyst said.
China's retail price inflation growth slowed to a year-on-year rise of 2.0 percent in the first half of this year from a year-on-year rise of 6.1 percent for the whole of 1996.

But the key resistance hindering the yuan's rise is coming from the People's Bank of China, the central bank, which has intervened to depress the yuan periodically since the national foreign exchange market was established in 1994, analysts said.
As a result, the yuan has only experienced a slight upward trend despite oversupply of U.S. dollars on the market since its establishment, they said.
The yuan rose 0.3 percent against the dollar in 1996 after a rise of 1.5 percent in 1995 and 2.9 percent in 1994, official figures showed.
The local unit was little changed in the first half of this year, ending at 8.2907 on June 28 against 8.2984 on December 31 last year.
"The key policy of the central bank has been to keep the yuan stable," the analyst said.
"With the yuan now at a relatively high level, fears of possible central bank intervention are justified," he said.
The profits of China's state export companies have also been squeezed due to the gain in the local currency, even though the rise was slight, analysts said.
A further rise in the yuan would make Chinese exports less competitive overseas, pressuring Beijing not to let the yuan rise too sharply, they said.
"The central government is unlikely to abandon the state exporters and leave them to solve their own problems," said the manager of a major Chinese export firm.
"To stabilise the yuan is one of the ways to support them before China's foreign trade system undergoes further changes," he said.
